translations.text: This is the life of the blessed John, the perfect monk, whose parents had a Gospel made for him in gold.
He completed his good life in perfection and admirable endurance, in peace, on the fourth day of the month of Mechir. May God bless us all. Amen.
For the life I am now going to tell you about is that of a man of God, a remarkable man who lived in our time.
Now there was a man living in the city of Rome who was extremely rich.
He was the governor of the city.
His name was Eutropius.
His wife's name was Theodora, and both of them had worshiped God since their childhood.
They had three sons.
They gave two of them high positions in the imperial palace.
The youngest, however, they entrusted to someone to be taught the things of God.
After this, he learned to read the writings of the scholars, and he was among them.
He was also instructed in the things of God, and he was devoted to the church, seeking God day and night.
One day, a brother who was a monk from the monastery in the interior, called the monastery of Those Who Do Not Sleep, passed by him. He wanted to go to Jerusalem to pray in the holy places.
He spoke with John near his house about the word of God.
John was greatly amazed as he looked at the brother, the monk, and his habit, and heard his sweet way of speaking and his thoughts, which were directed toward God like a fire.
John said, “My lord and father, where are you from? Or your monastery [?], or where is your monastery?”
The brother, the monk, said to him, “I live in the monastery of Those Who Do Not Sleep.
And, if God wills, I want to go to Jerusalem and pray there in the holy place. Then, by God's will, I will return to my own place again.”
And the monk told him about everything that John had told him about.
When John heard these words, he took the brother, the monk, by the hand and led him to a quiet place.
He bound him by solemn oaths, saying to him, “When you go to Jerusalem, my beloved brother, and return in peace, do not hide yourself from me.
And do not go to your monastery and leave me behind, for I hide nothing from you about my whole life. My parents love me very much, more than my brothers.
Indeed, they entrusted me to teachers.
And my father says, ‘I will give you high positions.’
Indeed, according to what is in his heart, he wants to give me seven more positions that are higher than his own.
And after this, he wants to arrange a marriage for me.

But I myself went to church and heard them reading a passage, saying, ‘All the glory of this world is something to laugh at,’ and, ‘Anyone who despises this world and follows Christ with an upright heart will scarcely be saved.’”
And especially, my brother, a sinner like me.
For this reason I beg you, my holy father, to take me with you to your monastery.
When the brother who was a monk heard this, he swore an oath: “When I return, I will take you with me to my monastery.”
Then they confirmed their agreement with one another, and each of them went to his monastery in peace.

After this, the blessed John considered the matter in his heart, saying, “First, let me go to my parents and have them provide me with a Gospel book to read, because I do not know Christ’s commandments.
And I will also find it in the place where I am going.”
He came to his parents’ house.

He offered them a pretext of this kind, saying, “Look, my parents, I am in [?] among my fellow students, because they are all at school with a gold Gospel book in each one’s hands, which their parents have provided for them to read.
But I am like a poor person among them who has neither a father nor a mother.”
John fell face down at his parents’ feet, saying, “I beg you, my very dear parents, provide me too with a Gospel book, so that I may have it in my hands and learn from it.”
When his mother heard this, she was very happy, because she wanted him to be well educated.
While she was still occupied with these things, she spoke to her husband, saying, “My lord and brother, have a gold Gospel book made for our son John.
Do not merely have it written, but decorate it beautifully with genuine stones of great value.”
At that moment his father gave orders.
He brought him five hundred gold coins and precious genuine stones and gave them to a master goldsmith.
He made the decoration for a Gospel book that had been written.
His father took it and gave it to his son John.
John took it and rejoiced over it.
And he was receiving instruction there with great sorrow.
He waited for the brother who was a monk to come, so that he could go with him.
After a few days, the brother who was a monk came because of the agreement they had made with one another.
When John saw the brother who was a monk, he was very glad and rejoiced. He greeted him with great joy.
He said to him, “My lord and father, I know my parents’ wishes and their love for me.
Especially my mother: if she hears of something like this concerning me, her tears will cause me even greater distress.
But I beg you, let us find a way to leave secretly.
And do not let anyone know about our departure.”
The monk said to him, “I will do as you wish.
And the Lord will fulfill for you what you have desired.”
Then John got up with the monk.
They went away secretly.
They came to the sea, looking for a boat to board.
John spoke to the boat's captain, saying, “I ask you, my brother, to settle the fare with us, so that you may take the two of us to the monastery of those who do not sleep.”
The boat's captain said to them, “Sit down until I have fitted out my boat, and we will sail, God willing.”
John said to the captain, “Tell me how much your fare is.”
The captain said to him, “The fare for my boat is one hundred solidi.”
Then John said to him, “I will give them to you.”
After John had said these things to the captain, he came to the place where the brother who was a monk was staying.

He said to him, “My father, the boat's fare is high, and the right thing for you is for us to leave quickly. Otherwise, they may come upon us, recognize us, and seize us, and we will be put to shame because we ran away secretly.”
Then John went into his house to his mother.
He said to her, “I beg you, my beloved mother. I know that you have fulfilled all my wishes.
There is just one more thing I lack, and it would be a source of pride for us both.”
She said to him, “Whatever you want, my son, ask me for it, and I will fulfill it for you.”
John said to his mother, “You know that all the boys who are with me at school have treated me to meals, not just once or twice, using what belongs to them, and I have eaten their food.
But I myself have had nothing with which to repay them for what they have done for me.
Because of this, shame has not allowed me to go to school again.”
His mother said to him, “I will do what you want for you.
When your father comes home at noon, I will have him give it to you, so that you can use it as you wish with your friends.”
Then, when his father came home at noon, she told him everything John had said to her.
He answered, saying, “I will give him everything he wants.
But let us assign a servant to him to watch over him, because he is a young boy. Otherwise, he might squander the money on evil things.”
They were pleased with the proposal. They called their son John and gave him the gold coins.
They also assigned the servant to him.

When John had received the gold coins, he came to the place where the monk was, together with the servant who accompanied him. He said to him, “My lord and brother, this servant whom you see belongs to me.”
Please let him stay with you while I go to my friends and ask them when they are coming to me.
Then the old monk understood that he was speaking to him about the ship’s captain.
But he had wanted to mislead him because of the servant who was accompanying him.
John took the hundred gold coins and went to the chief captain of the ship.
He said to him, “I beg you, my lord and brother, to prepare the ship so that we can leave quickly, my brother and I.”
When the captain heard this—that he wanted to leave secretly—he said to him, “I have already prepared my boat, and I have already told you once before that the fare for my boat is high.”
“But if you stay here until I have loaded my cargo onto the boat, I will take you aboard.”
John said, “I have already told you that I will pay you the fare you asked for.”
Immediately he brought out the hundred gold coins he had with him, rejoicing greatly.
He gave them to him, saying, “I will also give you the extra amount you told me about.”
“Now look, if the weather is favorable for you, do this for us for God’s sake: prepare the boat quickly so that we can leave secretly.”
When the captain of the boat heard this, he took the hundred gold coins from him, rejoicing greatly.
He said to John, “Go, bring your companion, and come back.”
“If it is God’s will, I will take good care of you.”
John returned.
He told the brother who was a monk everything that had happened to him.
After another two days, John said to the monk, “Get up, and let us go to the seashore, because this is the day when I will prepare lunch for my companions.”
“For I want to look for a little fish for them.”
They came to the seashore by God’s will.
A favorable wind arose.
The captain of the boat went and stood a short distance away on this side of the boat.
He sat down and beckoned to John and the other monk, saying, “Get up, come, and climb aboard.”
For they were anxious, wanting to separate themselves from the servant and leave him behind.
They had found no way to do so.
John said to the servant who was accompanying him, “Get up and go to the palace, to the lawyers, and see whether they have all gathered. Then come back and tell me quickly.”
“Look, I will be waiting for you.”
The servant went away.
They themselves immediately climbed aboard and launched the boat.
They arrived at the monastery by God’s will.
The servant returned to the seashore, but he did not find them.
He was deeply troubled in his heart, thinking, “Should I run away without telling my master?”
Then he said again, “I am afraid they might search for me, find me, and do terrible things to me.
But I will go and tell my masters. Perhaps they will search for him instead of me,
and I will be free from worry and at liberty.”
When his mother heard these things, she tore her clothes
and put dust on her head.
She wept bitterly, saying, “Woe to me, my beloved son John!
What has happened to you, my son, my sweetness? Woe to me, my son, for they have treated you with contempt! O John, my beloved son!
Woe to me!
Who has taken away the lamp of my heart?
I do not know!
Woe to me!
Who has taken away my beloved son, the beloved of my soul?
O John, my beloved son!
O light of my eyes!
I sent you to gain wisdom. I did not discover the fate that befell you!
Woe to me, my son, who is dear to everyone!
Woe to me, my sweet son, my beautiful face, full of every joy!
Woe to me, my [?] of the angels!
Woe to me! Oh, what will I do from this day onward?”
Likewise, his father too wept with sighing and anguish of heart, crying out and saying, “What has happened to you, O my beloved son?
I do not know what has happened to you so suddenly!”
When the seven days of mourning were over, during which the whole city mourned with them,
his father then got up, entered the palace, and told the king everything that had happened.
He begged him to send out an order throughout his kingdom so that they would search for him and perhaps find him.

When the king heard these things, he was deeply saddened and grieved at heart, because he loved him very much for his wisdom and knowledge, and because he used to eat with him at his tables, owing to his great affection for him.
Then the king sent out an order everywhere for soldiers to search for him. They went around everywhere but did not find him, and they returned to the palace.
His parents, after exhausting themselves searching for him without finding him, gave glory to God.
John came to the monastery with the other monk who was traveling with him.
He brought the golden Gospel book with him, which his parents had prepared for him.
He told the superior everything that had happened to the young boy John, and about his great faith in God.
The abbot said to the young boy, “My son, look, I see that you are small in stature and very fine in your deeds.”
“Now, my son, everyone who wishes to renounce this world spends forty days under probation, persevering. Afterward, they shave the hair from their heads and put the monastic habit on them.”

John said to him, “I implore you, my holy father, by the holy Trinity of one substance and by the prayers of the monastery, to shave my head today, because God knows that my heart aches with longing for the monastic life and the angelic habit.”
The archimandrite immediately agreed to pray over him, and he clothed him in the angelic habit.
His heart rejoiced greatly, and he pleaded with God day and night with great persistence, so that his prayers, his way of life, and his ascetic practices far surpassed those of many around him.
For it was as though he had spent six years persevering in this way and in the fear of God.
Indeed, he practiced great disciplines and many ascetic exercises.
When the archimandrite saw him, he was greatly amazed.
The archimandrite said to him, “My son, you are a young boy, and yet I see you undertaking many severe ascetic practices, mortifying your own body so that you cannot stand for prayer and fasting.”
For the hardship of abstinence makes a person even weaker.
But John did not give up the disciplines he was practicing.
When the devil, the hater of what is good, saw him, he became furiously angry. He could not bear him, seeing his great discipline, his ascetic practices, and the great honor he received.
Instead, he brought the memory of his parents into his mind.
Then he kept troubling him about this matter. Along with his many fasts and the nights he spent keeping vigil with perseverance,
his body grew weak, and he wasted away.
When the archimandrite saw him, he was astonished at the weakness that had come upon him, so that he was approaching death.
The archimandrite said to him, “Did I not tell you from the beginning that God does not ask anything of us beyond our strength?”
But you have become weak through this great deprivation.
John said to him, “Forgive me, my lord and father. It is not ascetic practice that has made me weak, but the memory of my parents that Satan has thrown into my heart, and the [?] in my home.
“There is also this other matter that you do not know about.
“If he keeps troubling me, I will go to them.
“And I trust in God and in your holy prayers that I will trample on all his power and not transgress what stands between me and God.”
And I also know that God will put him to shame.
The archimandrite said to him, “Did I not tell you that the devil has many tricks? But your crown of endurance is great.”
Then the elderly archimandrite wept over the blessed John, fearing that he might turn away from endurance.
The next day John got up and came to the archimandrite.
He fell at his feet and wept, saying, “My lord and father, I want to see my parents.

But I beg you not to cease praying steadfastly for me in my lowliness, so that God may bring me to a good fulfillment in endurance until I trample all the enemy’s power. Now give me permission to go.”
The archimandrite had all the brothers gather together to offer earnest prayers over him with many tears.
Then he sent him away, saying to him, “My son, go in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.
For he is the one who will walk with you, and he is the one who will guide you.”
John got up and took the gold Gospel book that his parents had prepared for him.
He begged the other elders to pray over him.
All of them together stretched out their hands over John’s head, saying, “The prayers of the saints will go with you, so that you may trample all the enemy’s power.”
At that very moment John got up and greeted all the brothers, saying, “Pray for me, my fathers and brothers.
I greet you all, the blessed people who received me among them and nurtured me with their holy teachings.
I am unworthy of you.”
After receiving the brothers’ farewell greeting, he left the monastery and went on his way.
When he was a little way outside the monastery, he turned his face back.
He looked at the monastery.
He wept bitterly and profusely.
Then, after weeping, he walked on until he approached the city.
While he was still walking, he met a weak man wearing clothes [?] and a worn-out cloak.
He said to him, “Greetings, my brother.
Come and walk with me.”
The brother said to him, “Sir, greetings, my brother.
I too was glad when I saw you. Let us walk together.”
John said to him, “My brother, I see that you are suffering greatly with these clothes and the rag you are wearing.
So I beg you to give them to me, and I will give you the clothes I am wearing.”
At once John stripped off the clothes he was wearing and gave them to the poor man.
And the poor man blessed John, John.
And, and they walked together until they reached the city that the poor man was entering.
Then they greeted one another, and each went his own way.
John reached his parents’ city.
He fell down on his face and wept.
He worshiped the Lord, saying, “My Lord Jesus Christ, do not abandon me.”
Then he entered his parents’ gateway. At the door of the house he fell down.
He worshiped the Lord, saying, “Lord Jesus Christ, here is my parents’ house; I have seen it. Give me strength until I trample on all the power of the enemy.”
Then John sat down at the entrance to the gateway of his parents’ house.
He slept until morning.
The next day the gatekeeper opened the gate as usual.
He saw John sitting at the entrance, wearing ragged clothes.
He said to him, “What is wrong with you, man? You dared to come into this place
and sit down wearing this filthy garment!
Get up and sit over here so I can clean my place before my master comes down. Otherwise,
if he sees you, he will quarrel with me.”
John said to him, “I beg you, my brother, do not throw me out, for I am a poor and wretched man.”
But the gatekeeper took pity on him.
He let him sit inside his parents’ gateway.
His parents came out in the morning.
And John saw them.
He wept so much that his body was soaked with his tears.
John rejoiced in his own thoughts, saying, “Look, my parents—
you have let me see them.
Now I also believe that you will let me tread upon all the power of the enemy.”
Immediately John wept with many tears, saying,
“My Lord Jesus Christ, do not abandon me.”
He stayed in his parents’ gateway for a whole year.
His father sent him food from his table every day, without knowing that he was his son.
His father would say, “As the Lord lives, my heart aches for this weak man, because he lives among these flies, naked like this, with no clothing on him, day and night.”
John remained in that place and did not want to leave it.
His father would say, “The Lord is merciful, and he will have mercy on us because of him.”
He put a small garment on him for God’s sake, for he was naked night and day. Then, one day,
his mother came downstairs.
She saw him in the wretched condition in which he was living, and smelled the stench of his body.
Her heart recoiled, and she vomited because of the filth of his body.
His body had become dry and shriveled because of the severe suffering caused by the ascetic practices he was undertaking and the anguish he was experiencing.
He was like a dying man.
She said to her servants, “Throw this man out of here, for I will not go upstairs
until you have thrown him out of here. I cannot pass by the place where this man is.”
Immediately the servants threw him out of the place where he was.
He got up from that place
and dragged himself a little farther away.
He did not go so far as to leave the place, but stayed close to the gateway.
When the doorkeeper saw him, he argued with him, saying, “Go away from here, man, because of my mistress, so that she will not see you. She would threaten me because of you.”
But John said to him, “I beg you, my brother, do not stop showing me the mercy you have shown me before today.
Instead, make me a little hut and a small place that I can go into, because of your mistress, so that she will not quarrel with you.”
The servant did not neglect the task, but made a little hut for him, and he stayed in it. His father sent him his daily provisions from his own table.
John would give whatever they sent him each day as charity to the poor and needy. He ate none of it except bread and salt.
The poor brothers in the city would come to him, and he fed them.
John’s body became extremely weak because of his many ascetic practices, so that each of his bones could be seen individually.
After ten years had passed, when the good God saw his great endurance, his ascetic practices, and his strength, the Lord appeared to him at night in a vision, saying to him, “Greetings, John!
In keeping with the name you were given, John, you too have become a virgin like him. Above all, you have left this world and all its glory behind and have come and followed me.
Look, the time of the hardships you have endured and the ascetic practices you have undertaken for my name has come to an end.
I have given you another three days in this world, until you come up to heaven to be with me and rest with my saints.”
John awoke from the vision.
He wept, saying, “I bless you, my Lord Jesus Christ.
I, who am utterly unworthy even to exist, am worthy to see the faces of the saints.
But I beg you, my Lord, on behalf of my parents: have mercy on them and forgive their sins, for you alone are without sin, the Lord God, the only Almighty.”
When the blessed John had said these things, he called the servant.
He said to him, “I know that you have treated me kindly.
Now I want to ask one more thing of you: go and tell your mistress this brief message that I will give you.”
The servant said to him, “Tell me everything you want, and I will tell her.”
John said to him, “Go and tell her, ‘This poor and weak man outside the gate, the one you said to throw out, says:’”
“I beg you, my lady: even if you despise me because I am a weak man, do this for me for God’s sake, and be so kind as to come to me here, for I have something to tell you.”
The servant went inside and told her everything John had said to him.
Then she said to him, “What does this beggar want to say to me?
I cannot bear to see him at all, or even to look at him.”
She went inside and told her husband and the members of her household what John had said to the servant.
Her husband said to her, “Go to him, my sister, and find out what he wants to tell you.
Do not despise him, for he too is a human being like us.
Indeed, it is the weak of the world whom God has chosen.”
But she did not want to go to him.
Again he sent to her a second time, saying, “I tell you that I have only three more days in this world.”
If you love me, let me speak with you and tell you this before I die.
“And [?] when I die.”
When she heard about his death, she got up and came down.
She said to her servants, “Go and bring him here to me.”
Then the servants identified him for her. His mother had not recognized him because of the many ascetic practices he performed.
John, her son, said to her, “What, then, is good for me to do to go up to God?”
As it is written, “Whatever you do for someone, it is for me that you do it.” So then,
I am a weak and poor man. I have nothing with which to repay you for what you and my lord, the ruler, have done for me, so that you may remember me by it after my death.
But get up and swear to me that you will do what I tell you,
and that you will not draw back from it.
And I will give you what the Lord assigned to me.
She said to him, “As the Lord lives, I will do as you tell me.”
But he said to her, “First swear an oath to me.”
And she swore to him.
He said to her, “I charge you by the living God: if I die, do not leave me stripped of the garment I am wearing. Rather, just as I am in it
now, bury me in it inside this little hut.”
When John had said these things, he brought out the golden Gospel book.
He gave it to her—the one that had been made for him before he became a monk—saying to her, “Let this be a remembrance for you in this age and the age to come.”
She kept turning it this way and that, saying, “This Gospel book resembles the Gospel book that my lord, my brother, made for my beloved son John.”
Then she remembered and wept bitterly, and her heart became greatly troubled.
She immediately went inside.
She showed it to her husband, saying, “Open this
and see whose it is.”
He recognized it immediately and said, “Truly, this is the Gospel book of our beloved son John, and it is no other than his.
Where did this weak man find this? Oh, surely
this man knows where our beloved son John is.”
Then the two of them came out, greatly agitated.
They came to the place where their son lay sleeping.
They said to him, “We adjure you by the holy, unchanging Trinity and by the great distress surrounding you to tell us the truth: where did you find this Gospel?”
For their hearts were troubled, and their tears were pouring onto the ground.
And they could not get up because of their abundant tears.
He said to them, “Have you not recognized who I am?”
They said to him, “How could we recognize you?”
He said to them, “I am John, your son, and this golden Gospel book is the one I asked you for.”
“I took it with me to the place where I was going.”
“But because I longed for the Lord and bore his holy power in this humble appearance,”
When his parents heard this, their hearts were deeply troubled. They could not hold back their tears, but wept bitterly.

Then they fell upon his chest and embraced him for a long time, from the first watch of the night until the sixth hour. All the nobles of the palace came and wept with them, because they had found John in such great abasement.
While his parents were lying upon him, the blessed John immediately opened his mouth and gave his spirit into the hands of God.
Oh, how great was the sorrow that arose throughout the whole city that day!
Indeed, loud cries arose among the nobles of the city, the rich and the poor, men and women, young and old.
They all came, wanting to see the blessed John.
His mother, overwhelmed by her grief and because of the commotion of the crowds, forgot the oath she had sworn to her son.
Then she had him stripped of the ragged clothes he was wearing and the other worn-out garments, and dressed him in a splendid robe worthy of royalty.
Immediately an angel came.
He touched his mother’s feet.
They struck against one another with trembling and severe spasms, because of the oath to her son John that she had forgotten.
Then his father came and saw her in torment. He said to her, “Truly, my sister, this has happened to you because of the oath to our son John that you disregarded.”
Then this matter troubled them.
And they removed the fine clothes from him.
They put the ragged clothes back on him as before.
And immediately the spasms in her feet stopped.

She raised her voice and wept in great anguish, saying, “Woe is me, my beloved son John! Oh, what has happened to you, the light of my eyes, that you have sunk to abasement as great as this and such great poverty?”
“Blessed is my womb, because it carried you, and my breasts, because they nourished you, O my holy son!”
The whole crowd marveled at the young man’s virtue, at how he had held himself firm with such great endurance, and they glorified God.
His parents buried him in the hut, as he had told them, and built a shrine over him.
They took everything they owned.
They distributed it to the poor and the needy.
Afterward his parents reached the end of a good life, giving glory to God, with the prayers of our holy fathers.
This is the struggle of Saint Joseph, in which he prevailed, because he girded himself.
He served the Lord Jesus Christ with great endurance, so that he might obtain favor for us before God and forgive us our many sins.
Through him, glory be to him and to his good Father and to the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.
Written on Mechir 23, in the first indiction, in the year 363 from the holy martyrs, [?].

I, the wretched sinner Victor, the least of deacons, son of the blessed [?], deacon, son of the blessed Eponychus, archdeacon of Saint Mercurius the great general, from Pollaton, wrote this book. Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom. On day [?].

Through the zeal and care of our God-loving brother, the [?] Zechariah, the deacon and monk of Saint Mercurius on the mountain of Tbo, he produced this book through his own labors and donated it to the monastery of Saint Mercurius on the mountain of Tbo,

where he lives, for the salvation of his soul, so that Saint Mercurius and all the other saints whose commemorations we have written in this book, each by name, may bless him with every spiritual and heavenly blessing. May he grant him endurance and save him from all the snares of the devil and of wicked people. May he enable him to carry out the service of the holy place and the office allotted to him, namely that of deacon and monk.

When he completes the course of this life, according to what is appointed for every person, may Saint Mercurius and the other saints whose names have been written in this book intercede with Christ for him. May he place him in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and may he receive an inheritance with the fathers of the community: Apa Palamon, Pachomius, Horsiesius, Apa Petronius, Theodore, and Apa Shenoute, and with all the saints. May he be worthy to hear:
“Well done, good and faithful servant! Because you were faithful in a few things, I will put you in charge of many. Enter into the joy of your Lord.”
Amen. So be it. 99.
